title: Pump rate in mL per hour from a prescription chart
blurb: Read a prescription chart row and set an infusion pump in mL per hour, including infusions over minutes.
question: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 1000 mL, IV, over 10 hours, start 0900. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?

teach.body: Formal rule: pump rate (mL per hour) = total volume (mL) ÷ time (hours). Plain English: how many mL must go in each hour to finish on time? Part A always has three IV items, each a prescription chart row (fluid, volume, route, duration, start time) and a box with "mL per hour" printed after it. You type the number only.

teach.caption: The start time tells you when, not how long. Ignore it for the rate.

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Ahmed on a medical ward
teach.body: Yusuf Ahmed, 70, has a chart row: 0.9% sodium chloride, 1000 mL, IV, over 10 hours, start 0900. Rate = 1000 ÷ 10 = 100 mL per hour. Sense-check: 100 mL each hour for 10 hours is 1000 mL, finishing at 1900. Type 100 in the box.

teach.caption: Minutes: divide by 60 to get hours, or multiply the volume by 60 and divide by the minutes.

teach.h: Minutes vs hours: 100 mL over 30 minutes
teach.caption: A short infusion over minutes always gives a rate bigger than the volume.

teach.text: Dividing by minutes, or by the start time. "Over 30 minutes" is 0.5 hours, so 100 mL runs at 200 mL per hour, not 3.33. And "start 0900" is a clock time: 1000 mL ÷ 9 = 111 is a classic slip.

teach.h: Hours and minutes as a decimal
teach.body: 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.5 hours, not 2.3. 3 hours 15 minutes is 3.25 hours. Change the minutes to a fraction of an hour (minutes ÷ 60) before you divide. Overnight infusions: from 2200 to 0600 is 2 hours to midnight plus 6 hours, which is 8 hours.

summary: You can now read a prescription chart row and calculate the pump rate in mL per hour, including infusions given over minutes or between two clock times. You can also sense-check the rate and type it in Pearson's number-only format.

A.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 1000 mL, IV, over 10 hours, start 0900. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
A.why: Rate = 1000 mL ÷ 10 hours = 100 mL per hour.

whyNot.0: This multiplies volume by time instead of dividing.
whyNot.1: This divides by the start time (0900), not the 10 hour duration.
whyNot.3: This divides by 100 instead of 10, a tenfold error.

A.q: Prescription: Hartmann's solution (compound sodium lactate), 500 mL, IV, start 1000, to finish at 1400. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
A.why: 1000 to 1400 is 4 hours. Rate = 500 ÷ 4 = 125 mL per hour.

whyNot.1: This counts 5 hours (1000, 1100, 1200, 1300, 1400) instead of the 4 hours between.
whyNot.2: This multiplies volume by time instead of dividing.
whyNot.3: This divides by the finish time (1400) as if it were hours.

A.q: Prescription: an antibiotic in 0.9% sodium chloride, 100 mL, IV, over 30 minutes, start 1200. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
A.why: 30 minutes = 0.5 hours. Rate = 100 ÷ 0.5 = 200 mL per hour.

whyNot.0: This divides by the minutes, not the hours.
whyNot.1: This halves the volume instead of doubling it.
whyNot.2: This multiplies the volume by the minutes.

B.q: A man is prescribed 1 unit of red cells, volume 300 mL, IV over 2 hours 30 minutes. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
B.why: 2 hours 30 minutes = 2.5 hours. Rate = 300 ÷ 2.5 = 120 mL per hour.

whyNot.0: This writes 2 hours 30 minutes as 2.3 hours.
whyNot.3: This rounds the duration up to 3 hours.

B.q: A patient on a mental health ward is prescribed Gelofusine 500 mL, IV over 90 minutes. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
B.why: 90 minutes = 1.5 hours. Rate = 500 ÷ 1.5 = 333.33, which is 333 mL per hour to the nearest whole number.

whyNot.0: This divides by the minutes, not the hours.
whyNot.1: This writes 90 minutes (1 h 30 min) as 1.3 hours.
whyNot.2: This rounds the duration up to 2 hours.

B.q: A client is prescribed 0.9% sodium chloride 1500 mL, IV over 12 hours, start 2000. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?

whyNot.1: This divides by the start time (2000) as if it were hours.
whyNot.2: This multiplies volume by time instead of dividing.
whyNot.3: This uses 10 hours instead of the 12 hours prescribed.

C.q: A child weighing 16 kg is prescribed red cells 15 mL/kg, IV over 4 hours. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
C.why: Volume = 15 × 16 = 240 mL. Rate = 240 ÷ 4 = 60 mL per hour.

whyNot.0: This divides the mL/kg by the hours and leaves out the weight.
whyNot.1: This is the total volume, not the hourly rate.
whyNot.3: This multiplies the volume by the hours.

C.q: A 1000 mL bag of 0.9% sodium chloride was prescribed over 8 hours and started at 0800 at the correct rate. At 1200 the prescriber asks for the remaining volume to run over the next 2 hours. What new rate should the pump be set to, in mL per hour?
C.why: Original rate = 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL per hour. By 1200 (4 hours) 500 mL has run, so 500 mL remains. New rate = 500 ÷ 2 = 250 mL per hour.

whyNot.0: This runs the whole 1000 mL over 2 hours and ignores the 500 mL already given.
whyNot.2: This is the original rate, unchanged.

C.q: A woman in labour is prescribed Hartmann's solution (compound sodium lactate) 1000 mL, IV over 12 hours. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
C.why: Rate = 1000 ÷ 12 = 83.33, which is 83 mL per hour to the nearest whole number.

whyNot.1: This rounds up; 83.33 rounds down to 83.
whyNot.2: This gives one decimal place; the stem asks for a whole number.
whyNot.3: This multiplies volume by time instead of dividing.

reteach.title: mL each hour
reteach.question: 500 mL is prescribed over 4 hours. How much goes in each hour?

blocks.h: Share the volume across the hours
blocks.body: 500 ÷ 4 = 125 mL per hour. Check: 125 × 4 = 500 mL. If the time is in minutes, change it to hours first.

blocks.text: Dividing 100 mL by 30 (the minutes) gives 3.33, which would take 30 hours to finish.

explain.h: Count the hours between two times
explain.body: From 1100 to 1600 is 5 hours (subtract: 16 − 11). Count gaps, not clock positions.

test.q: Prescription: 5% glucose, 250 mL, IV, start 1100, to finish at 1600. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
test.why: 1100 to 1600 is 5 hours. Rate = 250 ÷ 5 = 50 mL per hour.

whyNot.0: This multiplies volume by time instead of dividing.
whyNot.2: This counts 6 clock positions (1100 to 1600 inclusive) instead of the 5 hours between.

test.q: Prescription: an antibiotic in 0.9% sodium chloride, 50 mL, IV, over 20 minutes. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?

whyNot.1: This divides by the minutes, not the hours.
whyNot.2: This multiplies the volume by the minutes.
whyNot.3: This writes 20 minutes as 0.2 hours; it is 0.33 hours.

explain.body: 2200 to midnight is 2 hours; midnight to 0600 is 6 hours. Total 8 hours.

test.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 1000 mL, IV, start 2200, to finish at 0600. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
test.why: 2200 to 0600 is 8 hours. Rate = 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL per hour.

whyNot.0: This subtracts 6 from 22 and gets 16 hours.
whyNot.1: This counts only the 6 hours after midnight.

test.q: A man is prescribed 1 unit of red cells, volume 280 mL, IV over 3 hours 30 minutes. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
test.why: 3 hours 30 minutes = 3.5 hours. Rate = 280 ÷ 3.5 = 80 mL per hour.

whyNot.0: This writes 3 hours 30 minutes as 3.3 hours.
whyNot.3: This multiplies volume by time instead of dividing.
